nodes.title: Current-owner places and absolute height normalization
nodes.statement: For a number field K of degree d, identify the legacy InfinitePlace K ⊕ FinitePlace K with GlobalNumberFields.Place K by swapping the summands and identifying finite places with height-one prime ideals. Current infinite factors are v(x)^{mult(v)} and finite factors are the adic norms. Raise each current factor to 1/d to obtain the normalized factors used by H₂ and H_Q. The product formula is preserved. In E/K, the factor over w|v carries exponent d(w|v)=[E_w:K_v]/[E:K]. In particular H(x)=Height.mulHeight(x)^{1/d} for a nonzero tuple and h(x)=Height.logHeight(x)/d.
hypotheses: All fields, dimensions, normalizations and strict inequalities are as specified in the statement.
proofSteps: Use the native finite-place equivalence; the infinite factor retains its multiplicity before the degree root.
Use the product formula and the local-degree sum over each v to prove invariance under finite extension. This is the compatibility needed by the parent height, not a new place definition.
acceptance: For K=ℚ the root exponent is 1; at a complex place of a quadratic field it is 2/2, not 1/2.
The complex squared factor is not treated as an AbsoluteValue: its triangle estimate has exponent 2/d.

sources.match: The normalized places, continuation weights and coefficient-system hypotheses are those used by the absolute theorem. The native degree-normalization adapter is derived here.

nodes.title: Local exterior-power norm and determinant bounds
nodes.statement: For a p×n matrix whose rows are the p vectors over a normalized local field, the sup norm of its p-minors is at most the product of row sup norms at a nonarchimedean place; the Euclidean norm of those minors is at most the product of the p Euclidean vector norms at an archimedean place. Consequently H₂(span(x₁,…,x_p))≤∏ H₂(x_i) for independent vectors, and the wedge-coordinate sup version has the factor p^{p/2} when each input uses a coordinate sup norm.
hypotheses: All fields, dimensions, normalizations and strict inequalities are as specified in the statement.
proofSteps: At an archimedean place apply Cauchy–Binet to the Gram determinant and Hadamard; at finite places use the ultrametric determinant expansion.
Multiply with normalized local weights. The archimedean weights sum to 1, which gives one global p^{p/2}, rather than a power depending on K.
acceptance: For p=1 this is equality.
For p=n the wedge is a determinant, and its projective height is 1.

sources.match: Exterior-coordinate and Euclidean height conventions give the row-based wedge bound. Lemma 17.1 is the compound-family estimate, not a claim about column norms.

nodes.title: Plücker duality and orthogonal complement heights
nodes.statement: For a k-dimensional K-subspace U⊂Kⁿ, the signed complementary-minor map identifies its Plücker vector with that of the annihilator U⊥ for the standard bilinear pairing. Thus H₂(U⊥)=H₂(U); also H₂(U)=1 for k=0,n. This statement concerns bilinear annihilators over K, with Hermitian norms only after embedding at infinity.
hypotheses: All fields, dimensions, normalizations and strict inequalities are as specified in the statement.
proofSteps: Choose an invertible basis minor and row-reduce. The kernel matrix has complementary minors equal up to one common nonzero scalar and signs.
Signed coordinate permutation preserves every local sup or Euclidean norm; projective invariance cancels the common scalar.
acceptance: For a rational line generated by (2,3), its perpendicular line generated by (−3,2) has the same H₂=√13.

sources.match: The signed complementary Plücker coordinates of an annihilator have the same local norms. The packet uses this argument for the dual-space pairing, without identifying arbitrary number-field lattices as self-dual.

nodes.title: Intersection and sum inequality for subspace heights
nodes.statement: For subspaces U,V⊂Kⁿ, H₂(U∩V) H₂(U+V)≤H₂(U)H₂(V). This includes nontrivial intersections, and is stronger than applying the exterior product bound only in the disjoint case.
hypotheses: All fields, dimensions, normalizations and strict inequalities are as specified in the statement.
proofSteps: Use a common basis A of U∩V and complements B,C. At each archimedean place pass to the quotient by span(A); Gram–Schmidt gives volume(A,B,C) volume(A)≤volume(A,B)volume(A,C).
At a finite place use a unit minor of A after scaling and elimination; the induced quotient sup norm gives the corresponding nonarchimedean determinant inequality.
Multiply local inequalities, cancel the projective scalars, and use the product formula. The lecture notes quote the inequality; the local quotient proof is the required development.
acceptance: If U⊂V both sides are equal.
In ℚ³, U=span(e₁,e₂) and V=span(e₁,e₂+e₃) give 1·1≤1·√2.

sources.locator: Corollary 2.3.11 and the following paragraph, p. 39
sources.match: This gives the subspace intersection/sum inequality. The requested constant-one Euclidean version is derived by a local quotient-wedge argument; the quoted sup-height version is not silently used with a different metric.

nodes.title: Northcott for fixed-degree subspaces
nodes.statement: For n,k,D and B fixed, only finitely many k-subspaces U⊂Q̄ⁿ with [field of definition of U:ℚ]≤D and H₂(U)≤B exist. A Plücker chart with a nonzero coordinate makes every ratio a scalar of degree≤D and absolute multiplicative height≤B; the injective Plücker map then reduces to fixed-degree scalar Northcott.
hypotheses: All fields, dimensions, normalizations and strict inequalities are as specified in the statement.
proofSteps: Choose one of finitely many nonzero Plücker coordinates and divide by it.
Bound the heights of coordinate ratios by the Plücker sup height, which is≤H₂; use the parent fixed-degree scalar Northcott and Plücker reconstruction.
acceptance: The degree bound is essential: roots of unity give infinitely many lines (1,ζ) of H₂=√2.
A fixed ambient number field gives a special case using native fixed-field Northcott.

sources.match: These are the subspace-height conventions. Finiteness is an independent derivation using a nonzero Plücker chart and native scalar Northcott; these pages are not cited as a proof of Northcott.

nodes.title: Primitive Plücker coordinates and rational covolume
nodes.statement: For a rational k-subspace U⊂ℚⁿ, L=U∩ℤⁿ is saturated and has rank k. Every specified ℤ-basis b of L extends to a basis of ℤⁿ, hence the gcd of the k-minors of b is 1. Therefore H₂(U)=√det(Gram(b))=covol(L) in U⊗ℝ. This constructs the lattice and proves primitivity, rather than assuming an arbitrary integral basis is primitive.
hypotheses: All fields, dimensions, normalizations and strict inequalities are as specified in the statement.
proofSteps: Saturation follows from m x∈U⇒x∈U for nonzero integer m. Use the prescribed-basis extension theorem, and expand determinant±1 along the first k columns to obtain an integral combination of minors equal to±1.
Finite local height factors are then 1; Cauchy–Binet supplies the infinite factor.
acceptance: For the line (2,3) the primitive basis gives √13; using twice this vector without dividing its common factor would wrongly give 2√13.

sources.match: The Euclidean subspace height motivates the normalization. The covolume identity is derived using the existing GN.0 Gram determinant and mixed-embedding normalization contracts, rather than attributed to these pages.

nodes.title: Full S-unit logarithmic image
nodes.statement: Let S contain all infinite places and finitely many finite places of K. The map u↦(log|u|_v)_{v∈S}, with degree-normalized factors, has torsion kernel and image a full lattice in Σ_v z_v=0. In particular every vector of that hyperplane is within a K,S-dependent bounded sup distance of some unit logarithm. Native finite generation alone does not imply fullness.
hypotheses: All fields, dimensions, normalizations and strict inequalities are as specified in the statement.
proofSteps: Use native ordinary Dirichlet for the infinite-place kernel. Finite class-group torsion makes each chosen finite prime power principal; its generator is an S-unit with one nonzero finite valuation direction.

The principal-power and finite-index valuation adapter is requested as a Part II of current GlobalNumberFields Layer 2, using the already existing finite class group. No class-group finiteness theorem is replanned.

The finite valuation coordinates form a discrete subgroup; their zero fibre is the discrete ordinary-unit logarithmic lattice. This proves discreteness of the full image. The independent valuation directions and ordinary Dirichlet give full rank in the product-formula hyperplane, with torsion kernel.
A fundamental parallelepiped of the resulting full lattice is bounded, giving the approximation statement.
acceptance: For ℚ with S={∞,p}, the logarithmic image is ℤ(log p,−log p).
For imaginary quadratic K and only infinite places, the hyperplane and free unit rank are both zero.

sources.match: The scalar approximation uses a full logarithmic S-unit lattice. Native ordinary Dirichlet, the S-valuation kernel and the requested principal-power adapter supply its directions and discreteness.

nodes.title: Absolute rescaling with one distinguished place
nodes.statement: Let A_v>0 equal 1 outside a finite set containing all infinite places, with A=∏A_v≥1; fix v₀ and ε>0. There are a finite extension E/K and β∈E* with |β|_w≤A_v^{d(w|v)} for w|v≠v₀ and |β|_w≤((1+ε)A_{v₀}/A)^{d(w|v₀)} for w|v₀. The variant without a distinguished place uses ∏A_v>1 and gives |β|_w≤A_v^{d(w|v)} everywhere.
hypotheses: All fields, dimensions, normalizations and strict inequalities are as specified in the statement.
proofSteps: Approximate a large multiple of the balanced target vector of logarithms by the S-unit lattice. Reserve the positive log(1+ε) margin at v₀ and enough negative margin elsewhere to absorb the bounded error.
Adjoin a k-th root of that unit; divide all errors by k and check the local-degree weights. This is why the scalar may require a finite extension.
acceptance: When A=1 and all A_v=1 one may take β=1.
A zero ε boundary is not inferred from approximation.

sources.match: This gives the rescaling weights and their product-formula compatibility.
The logarithmic approximation lemma supplies an algebraic scalar with the required controlled local rescalings.

nodes.title: Unitary symmetric-power metric
nodes.statement: On Symʳ(Kᵐ), let e^I be the image of a tensor word of multiplicity I, identified with its symmetric average. For v=Σ a_I e^I use ‖v‖²=Σ |a_I|²/binomial(r;I) at infinity. In the dual basis ε_I, ‖Σ b_I ε_I‖²=Σ binomial(r;I)|b_I|². The associated ordinary polynomial is f(x)=ℓ(x^⊗r)=Σ c_I x^I with c_I=binomial(r;I)b_I; hence its dual squared norm is Σ |c_I|²/binomial(r;I). Finite places use the prescribed adelic sup norm. The tensor construction is unitary-invariant; unweighted coefficient norm is not.
hypotheses: All fields, dimensions, normalizations and strict inequalities are as specified in the statement.
proofSteps: Average the binomial(r;I) orthonormal tensor words with each multiplicity. The average has squared norm 1/binomial(r;I), and different multiplicities are orthogonal.
The dual basis has reciprocal squared weights. Expand x^⊗r=Σ binomial(r;I)x^I e^I to identify ordinary polynomial coefficients; this accounts for the extra multinomial in the pairing.

Restrict a unitary tensor-power map to the symmetric tensors. Compare all weighted norms to coefficient norms with explicit multinomial factors; the corrected absolute-basis argument remains a separate gap.
acceptance: For m=2,r=2 the vector e₁e₂ has squared norm 1/2; its dual basis vector has squared norm 2 and corresponds to the polynomial 2XY. The ordinary polynomial XY has dual squared norm 1/2.
The displayed rotation of e₁² preserves norm one.

sources.match: The printed unweighted symmetric-power metric fails the rotation test. The replacement is derived from the tensor-product metric, distinguishing coordinates in the dual basis from coefficients of the ordinary polynomial.

nodes.title: From corrected absolute bases to twisted Minkowski
nodes.statement: Assume the corrected absolute small-basis theorem for adelic Hermitian spaces, with the Roy–Thunder determinant/metric conventions. Apply it to the n coordinate forms at every place, then pass to the algebraic-closure infima. The resulting statement is the parent absolute Minkowski theorem n^{−n/2}Δ Q^{−α}≤∏_{i=1}^n λ_i(Q)≤2^{n(n−1)/2}Δ Q^{−α}, with α=Σ_{v,i}c_{iv}. The lower bound follows directly from local determinants and does not need the unread erratum.
hypotheses: All fields, dimensions, normalizations and strict inequalities are as specified in the statement.
proofSteps: For independent nearly minimizing vectors bound each local determinant by the product of local form maxima, with the normalized archimedean factor n^{n/2}; multiply to obtain the lower inequality.

For the upper inequality match the adelic twisted box to the corrected absolute-basis theorem and rescale via the preceding lemma. A fixed-field Minkowski theorem is insufficient because λ_i is taken over Q̄.
The upper-bound source is a recorded gap until the full 1999 erratum proof is obtained and its constants propagated.
acceptance: Prove the lower determinant inequality separately; mark the upper inequality conditional on the unread corrected-basis proof, with no discriminant term.

nodes.title: Successive infima, gap subspaces and Galois descent
nodes.statement: For the parent finite-support, extension-compatible and Galois-invariant twisted height, 0<λ₁(Q)≤⋯≤λ_n(Q)<∞, and independent near minimizers exist for every positive error. If λ_k<λ_{k+1}, the span of all vectors of height<λ_{k+1} has dimension k and is K-defined. Under all EF (8.1)–(8.9), Q>C₂ and λ₁(Q)≤Q^−δ, any p distinct indices satisfy Q^(−p−1/2)≤∏λ_{i_j}(Q)≤Q^(n−p+1/2), and some 1≤k<n satisfies λ_k(Q)≤Q^(−δ/(n−1))λ_{k+1}(Q). No infimum is asserted to be attained.
hypotheses: All fields, dimensions, normalizations and strict inequalities are as specified in the statement.
proofSteps: The parent coordinate lower bound and a coordinate basis give positivity and finiteness; the infimum definition gives independent near minimizers.
For a strict adjacent gap, all intermediate threshold spans coincide and have dimension k. Galois invariance makes their common span K-defined by the parent descent input.

In the semistable normalized setting use the coordinate lower bound λ₁>Q^(−1−1/(3n)) and absolute Minkowski to bound each product of p infima. The same determinant estimates give λ_n>1. Choose the smallest adjacent ratio, whose (n−1)-st power is at most λ₁/λ_n.
acceptance: Use strict adjacent gaps only. A span of near minimizers must be independent of their choices before invoking Galois descent.

sources.match: The near-minimum span, adjacent-minimum gap and Galois invariance are used with Q>C₂ and the prescribed product bounds.

nodes.title: Restriction heights and subspace-height lower bounds
nodes.statement: Assume the distinct form family contains X₁,…,X_n. For a basis g of a k-subspace T and all its distinct nonzero restricted determinants θ₁,…,θ_u, put A=√binomial(n,k)H_L H₂(T). Over a common number field E, ∏_w max_j|θ_j|_w≤A and ∏_w min_j|θ_j|_w≥A^(1−binomial(R,k)), where R bounds the number of distinct forms. Under all EF (8.1)–(8.9), Q>C₂, λ₁(Q)≤Q^−δ and λ_k(Q)≤Q^(−δ/(n−1))λ_{k+1}(Q), the gap subspace T=T_k(Q) satisfies H₂(T)>Q^(δ/(3R^n)). A mere strict adjacent gap is insufficient.
hypotheses: All fields, dimensions, normalizations and strict inequalities are as specified in the statement.
proofSteps: Cauchy–Binet bounds each restricted determinant by the Plücker norm of g times the exterior coefficient norm. Because the coordinate forms are in the family, every subminor is included in its determinant-height bound. Multiply to obtain the maximum estimate.
The product formula for θ₁⋯θ_u bounds the product of local minima below by the maximum product to the power 1−u; u≤binomial(R,k) gives the stated weaker estimate.

Choose weight-minimizing independent restrictions on T. Semistability bounds their total weight by zero. Apply determinant bounds to k independent near minimizers and the quantitative adjacent gap to get the selected-determinant product≤Q^(−δ/(2n)). Combining with the preceding minimum bound and Q>C₂ gives the strict height lower bound.
acceptance: The estimate requires the semistable assumptions; a positive-weight exceptional subspace is not a counterexample to the conditional statement.

sources.match: The source uses every independent restricted coordinate tuple. Their determinant-product upper and lower bounds lead to the strict lower bound on the exceptional subspace height.

nodes.title: Nearly minimizing bases with concentrated archimedean slack
nodes.statement: Fix v₀ and ε>0. Independent near minimizers can be individually rescaled so that |L_{iv}(x_j)|_v≤n^{−s(v)}Q^{c_{iv}} away from v₀, while at v₀ the bounds are ((1+ε)nλ_j(Q))^{d(w|v₀)}Q^{c_{iw}}. Here s(v)=[K_v:ℝ]/[K:ℚ] at infinity and zero at finite places; after extension the same exponents are multiplied by d(w|v).
hypotheses: All fields, dimensions, normalizations and strict inequalities are as specified in the statement.
proofSteps: Take a common finite field for the independent vectors. For each vector set A_v from its actual local twisted maximum and apply distinguished-place rescaling.
The product of the A_v is its twisted height; use the near-minimum bound. The independent scalar multiplications preserve independence.
acceptance: The distinguished place is finite and has zero weights and coordinate forms. Multiply the rescaling factors to recover the global near-minimum bound.

sources.match: The two-sided rescaling estimate compares the compound height and ordinary Euclidean height on the distinguished minimum space.

nodes.title: Adelic approximation of elimination coefficients
nodes.statement: Given algebraic θ₁,…,θ_{t−1}, a distinguished place v₀ and ε>0, there are algebraic γ₁,…,γ_t with γ_t≠0: |γ_i|_v≤t^{−s(v)} at archimedean v≠v₀ and≤1 at finite v≠v₀; at v₀, |γ_i−θ_iγ_t|_w≤1 and |γ_t|_w≤((1+ε)^t2^{t²})^{d(w|v₀)}. The formulation is after a finite extension containing all coefficients.
hypotheses: All fields, dimensions, normalizations and strict inequalities are as specified in the statement.
proofSteps: Apply absolute Minkowski to a unipotent system with last coordinate γ_t and the error forms γ_i−θ_iγ_t.
Choose the first nonzero vector after absolute rescaling; if γ_t=0 the remaining coordinates have a strictly too small global product, contradicting the product formula.
Track the archimedean factors and use the generous 2^{t²} bound for the successive-minima product.
acceptance: The last coefficient must be nonzero; test the product-formula contradiction when all error coordinates are too small and that coefficient vanishes.

sources.match: This is the height redistribution lemma for an ordered basis and prescribed diagonal parameters; its comparisons precede the triangular change.

nodes.title: Davenport elimination along a Galois-defined flag
nodes.statement: In the parent semistable setting, with distinguished nonarchimedean v₀ where c_{iv₀}=0 and L_{iv₀}=X_i, fix Q≥1. Choose ε>0 with (1+ε)²λ_i<λ_{i+1} at every strict gap and n·2^{n²}(1+ε)^{n+1}<3^{n²}, and independent g_i with H_Q(g_i)≤(1+ε/2)λ_i. There are a finite extension E/K, a permutation π and a basis h_j preserving every initial span of the g_j, such that |L_{iw}(h_j)|_w≤n^{−s(w)}Q^{c_{iw}} for w not over v₀, and |L_{π(i),w}(h_j)|_w≤[3^{n²}min(λ_i,λ_j)]^{d(w|v₀)} for w over v₀. Here s(w) is the normalized infinite local degree and zero at finite places.
hypotheses: All fields, dimensions, normalizations and strict inequalities are as specified in the statement.
proofSteps: Select pivots in K-defined annihilators of the flag blocks; use Gaussian elimination in increasing block order.
Approximate each elimination coefficient by the preceding adelic lemma, preserving previous pivots. Multiply the local error bounds and sum the geometric losses to obtain 3^{n²}.
acceptance: Equal infima form one block; inventing a gap inside an equal block would make the descent argument invalid.

sources.match: The absolute Davenport argument produces the triangular basis with controlled local norms.
This is the particular redistribution contract needed for the compound-minimum argument.

nodes.title: Compound heights, truncated weights and the final wedge
nodes.statement: Put p=n−k and N=binomial(n,p). Index the compound coordinates I_j lexicographically and set ĉ_jv=Σ_{i∈I_j}c_iv and ν_j=∏_{i∈I_j}λ_i. These ν_j are not generally increasing, although ν_N and ν_{N−1} are the largest and second largest. Under EF (11.8)–(11.9), truncate the distinguished-place last product to ν_{N−1} as in (11.15). Away from v₀ the compound weights sum to zero, max|ĉ|≤(n−1)max c and their summed maxima are≤n−1; at v₀ their sum is≤−δ/n and max|ĉ|≤n. The inverse compound coefficient height is≤H_L^(R^n), and the N−1 wedge span has height H₂(T_k(Q))>Q^(δ/(3R^n)). Separately, for the untruncated compound system sort the products as μ₁≤⋯≤μ_N. Its infima satisfy N^(−npN)μ_j≤λ̂_j≤p^(p/2)μ_j.
hypotheses: All fields, dimensions, normalizations and strict inequalities are as specified in the statement.
proofSteps: Apply the Davenport basis estimate to the lexicographic wedges. Keep the permutation of compound coordinates; the last two products have ratio λ_k/λ_{k+1}.

At v₀ replace the largest product by the second largest. The product of all ν_j is (∏λ_i)^binomial(n−1,p−1), so the quantitative gap makes the distinguished weight sum negative. The product bounds control its absolute coordinates.
Use complementary minors and the determinant-height identity to bound the inverse compound matrices; exterior duality identifies the N−1 wedge-span height with the k-gap subspace height.

For the untruncated comparison use independent nearly minimizing wedges to bound λ̂_j≤p^(p/2)μ_j. Absolute Minkowski in dimensions n and N bounds the product of λ̂_j/μ_j below, and the upper bounds on the other ratios give the weaker explicit lower factor N^(−npN).
acceptance: Check N=binomial(n,n−k), lexicographic compound coordinates, the zero weight sums away from v₀ and the strictly negative sum at v₀ separately.

sources.match: The truncation targets the distinguished final compound directions. Lexicographic products are separated from the sorted compound-minimum list; Lemma 17.3 has lower factor N^(−npN).

nodes.title: Small vectors in number-field linear kernels
nodes.statement: Let K have degree d and discriminant D_K, C_K=|D_K|^{1/(2d)}, and let A be an M×N matrix of rank M<N. There are L=N−M independent vectors x_j∈O_K^N in its kernel with ∏_j H₂(x_j)≤(√N C_K)^L H₂(row A). Consequently one has H₂(x)≤√N C_K H₂(row A)^{1/L} for some x≠0. Since H₂(row A)≤∏_iH₂(A_i), this implies the parent Lemma 13.1 bound for U<N possibly dependent equations, using denominator N−U. The finite-place primitive row-minor ideal is already incorporated into H₂(row A), and must not be divided out a second time.
hypotheses: All fields, dimensions, normalizations and strict inequalities are as specified in the statement.
proofSteps: Use the lower-tier adelic-minima and normalized ball-product section contracts requested from GN.1. For a kernel basis Y, BV Theorem 7 gives the adelic box volume≥H₂(Y)^{−d}|D_K|^{−L/2} in Haar measure with covolume-one K^L.

BV Theorem 3 bounds (∏λ_j)^d times that volume by 2^{dL}. Theorem 8 converts its independent witnesses to integral vectors with ∏H∞(x_j)≤[(2/π)^{r₂/d}C_K]^L H₂(Y). Complementary minors and the product formula identify H₂(Y)=H₂(row A). Finally H₂(x_j)≤√N H∞(x_j), and (2/π)^{r₂/d}≤1 gives the displayed bound.
Take the least-height vector among the N−M independent vectors. EF only needs the half-rank corollary, but the primitive ideal and discriminant are retained.
acceptance: A rank-deficient matrix must first be replaced by independent rows; an N/2 bound counts independent conditions, not a claimed exact rank.

sources.match: The kernel-lattice determinant and adelic section-volume argument are the number-field Siegel input.
The section-volume bound applies to products of Euclidean balls. Its conjectural extension to arbitrary convex bodies is unused.
This is the coefficient-vector application with its field-dependent constant. Real self-dual lattice statements alone do not prove it.

nodes.title: Coefficient count and simultaneous weighted-tail constraints
nodes.statement: For m blocks of N variables of degrees r_h, the number of monomials is V=∏_h binomial(r_h+N−1,N−1). For each place in a finite set S₀, the proportion of exponent tuples outside the weighted concentration band is≤exp(−mε²/2). Hence m>2ε^{−2}log(2|S₀|+2) leaves fewer than V/2 simultaneous linear coefficient conditions.
hypotheses: All fields, dimensions, normalizations and strict inequalities are as specified in the statement.
proofSteps: Treat uniform weak compositions in each block as independent variables; normalize the weighted sums using the actual local weight range.
Apply the bounded-variable exponential-moment estimate and union bound. Count compositions directly: no extra product of block degrees multiplies V.
Each condition is coefficient extraction after the local linear substitution; bound its coefficient height by ((6N²)^s C_v)^{Σr_h}.
acceptance: Count linear conditions by a union bound across the actual finite representative systems. The count must be strictly less than V/2 before invoking Siegel.

sources.match: The multihomogeneous coefficient-space count and weighted high-derivative conditions leave enough coefficients for the small auxiliary polynomial.

nodes.title: Simplex discretization of normalized local weights
nodes.statement: Let c∈ℝⁿ, Σc_i=0, γ=max c_i>0 and 0<ε≤1/10. Set b_i=1−c_i/γ, so b_i≥0 and Σb_i=n. The bins (⌊b_i/ε⌋)_i have at most binomial(⌊n/ε⌋+n,n)≤(3/ε)^n values. Choosing one actual weight vector per occupied bin gives coordinate error<ε. Together with at most Rⁿ ordered local form systems this gives |S₀|≤(3R/ε)^n, the count used in EF §14.
hypotheses: All fields, dimensions, normalizations and strict inequalities are as specified in the statement.
proofSteps: The printed cube [−1,1]ⁿ is false for normalized zero-sum weights. The b-coordinates put them in the simplex of mass n.
Stars-and-bars counts all floor tuples of sum≤⌊n/ε⌋. Use binomial(a+n,n)≤(e(a+n)/n)^n and e(1+ε)≤3.
Take representatives from occupied bins; do not replace them by arbitrary weight vectors which might violate normalization. The ε used in §14 is inside this range.
acceptance: For n=3, c=(−2,1,1) has γ=1 and b=(3,0,0); it is permitted.
This argument does not assert the same bound for every ε<1; the unused larger-ε formulation remains outside this repair.

sources.match: The zero-sum weights are discretized on a simplex, correcting the false cube assertion. The repaired count is used only in the ε≤1/10 range of the quantitative application.

nodes.title: Auxiliary polynomial with half-rank height control
nodes.statement: For the compound system with N=binomial(n,n−k), positive block degrees r_h and 0<ε≤1/10, assume m>2nε^−2 log(4R/ε). There is a nonzero multihomogeneous P such that, for every normalized derivative of weighted order≤2mε, its transformed coefficient of a monomial j vanishes when Σ_{h,l}ĉ_lv j_hl/r_h>4mnεγ_v away from v₀, or when Σ_{h,l}ĉ_l,v₀(Q_h)j_hl/r_h>−mδ/(nN)+4mnε at v₀. Here γ_v=max_i c_iv and the distinguished weights may depend on Q_h. One has H₂(P)≤C_K(2^(3n)H_L^(R^n))^Σr_h; the product of local maxima of the transformed derivative coefficient norms is≤C_K(2^(6n)H_L^(2R^n))^Σr_h. C_K depends on the fixed coefficient field and not on the large degree parameter.
hypotheses: All fields, dimensions, normalizations and strict inequalities are as specified in the statement.
proofSteps: The finite-net bound makes the number of imposed coefficient conditions less than half the coefficient dimension. Apply the number-field kernel theorem with this half-rank inequality.

For a derivative of weighted order≤2mε and a net-bin error<ε, translate the representative tail threshold to the enlarged threshold above at every original place. The prohibited coefficients have high weight.

Bound substitution and derivative coefficient losses using the inverse compound matrices. Multiply the local bounds, retaining C_K; only the later choice of a sufficiently large degree absorbs that fixed constant.
acceptance: The polynomial must be nonzero and satisfy every original place constraint, including those represented by a net bin. Keep C_K independent of the degree parameter.

sources.match: The forbidden derivatives have high weighted order. The half-rank estimate and transformed derivative bounds require m>2nε^−2 log(4R/ε), with the stated field and form-height factors.

nodes.title: Nonzero jet and product-formula contradiction
nodes.statement: In the semistable case with 0<δ≤1, take the auxiliary polynomial, compound bases and separated parameters of EF §14. Choose ε with 10nε<δ/(nN). The nonzero evaluated jet supplied by the parent grid/Roth inputs has global product at most (eN²2^{7n}H_L^{2Rⁿ})^{Σr_h}(Q₁^{mr₁})^{10nε−δ/(nN)}, after choosing r₁ sufficiently large to absorb C_K. For Q₁ above the stated source threshold this product is<1, contradicting the product formula.
hypotheses: All fields, dimensions, normalizations and strict inequalities are as specified in the statement.
proofSteps: Balance the degrees so Q_h^{r_h} lie between Q₁^{r₁} and (Q₁^{r₁})^{1+ε}; choose the integer grid jet using the parent strict vanishing threshold.
At finite places bound every term ultrametrically; at infinity account for the derivative coefficient and substitution losses.

Multiply all local bounds. The negative exponent comes from the distinguished compound coordinate, while all other weight sums cancel. Take the degree parameter large only after Q and the fixed-field constant are fixed.
acceptance: The jet is nonzero, so its global absolute-value product is 1. Verify the negative exponent and the strict upper bound less than 1 after absorbing C_K.

sources.match: The gap selects degrees adapted to separated Q-values and converts the auxiliary-polynomial derivative bound into the high-index conclusion.

nodes.title: Restriction and quotient slopes of the weight flag
nodes.statement: For any K-defined proper subspace T, choose at each place the lexicographically least restricted independent basis I_v(T) in the order of increasing c_iv. These selected weights give the restriction. Eliminate their forms by the chosen minor to obtain triangular quotient forms indexed by the complementary indices. For U⊃T the quotient weight is w(U)−w(T). On each consecutive block of the canonical weight flag, subtract its mean slope to obtain a semistable system. The slopes strictly decrease. The last proper flag member, rather than the first positive-slope member, is the unique smallest-dimensional maximizer of w(U)/(n−dim U).
hypotheses: All fields, dimensions, normalizations and strict inequalities are as specified in the statement.
proofSteps: The weighted independent-basis rule realizes the minimum defining w_v(T). Supermodularity of the global weight identifies the canonical flag maximizers.
Construct the quotient forms by triangular elimination, not by simply restricting unmodified complementary forms. Verify the quotient identity for each U containing T and extension invariance.
For consecutive canonical blocks use the maximality of the flag to bound all proper subspace slopes. Subtract the block mean, yielding weight≤0 and thus semistability.
The final maximizing ratio follows from the strictly decreasing slopes; the dimension-weight expression stops at n−1.
acceptance: For each intermediate U containing T verify the quotient weight formula. Mean shifts must make every block semistable and the dimension-weighted slopes sum correctly.

sources.match: Weighted lexicographic bases define the filtration. Each quotient uses descended triangularly eliminated forms; the proper last term is the exceptional space.

nodes.title: Asymptotics of successive infima on semistable blocks
nodes.statement: For a semistable n-dimensional twisted system with total weight zero and any δ>0, eventually λ₁(Q)>Q^{−δ/(2n)} and λ_n(Q)≤Q^δ. On a block with mean weight μ, undoing the shift gives log λ_i(Q)/log Q→−μ. In the full flag, the exponent α in the Minkowski product is Σ(block dimension)·μ; cumulative flag dimensions would give the wrong sum.
hypotheses: All fields, dimensions, normalizations and strict inequalities are as specified in the statement.
proofSteps: The semistable interval theorem prevents arbitrarily large Q with a small first minimum: its finitely many bounded multiplicative intervals cannot contain an unbounded sequence.
Use the absolute Minkowski product and monotonicity to bound the largest minimum. Dimension one follows directly from the product formula.
Induct along the flag using restricted/quotient comparisons. Match the slopes in increasing minimum order, and verify that their dimension-weighted sum is the total exponent.
acceptance: In dimension one recover the product formula directly. Higher dimensions use finitely many bounded intervals, rather than assuming infima are attained.

sources.match: The fixed-space proof combines the quotient filtration with a height gap and scalar rescaling. The low-minimum space agrees with the proper filtration term.

nodes.title: Quantitative height of the canonical weight flag
nodes.statement: Let B=max_L H₂(L) over the distinct individual linear forms. For each member T_i of the canonical weight flag, H₂(T_i)≤B^(4^n). The intermediate hyperplane estimate is B^((n−1)^2). For a k-space use p=n−k and the compound dimension N=binomial(n,p): each compound form has height≤B^p, and p(N−1)^2≤4^n. In the normalized coordinate-form setting of EF §18, B≤√nH_L, so H₂(T_i)≤(√nH_L)^(4^n). B and H_L are different heights.
hypotheses: All fields, dimensions, normalizations and strict inequalities are as specified in the statement.
proofSteps: Use the asymptotic flag and successive-infima estimates to obtain the hyperplane height bound in terms of the maximum individual form height B.
Pass to the untruncated compound system and its asymptotic final hyperplane. Exterior duality gives equal subspace heights; the exterior local norm bounds each compound form by B^p.
Use p(N−1)^2≤4^n. When coordinate forms are present, their determinant-height bound controls each coefficient and gives B≤√nH_L.
acceptance: For B=1 the flag bound forces height 1; for n=3 the exponent is 64. H_L=1 alone does not imply B=1.

sources.match: These are the compound-coordinate bounds and the filtration-height induction. B bounds individual form heights; B≤√n H_L in the normalized system.

nodes.title: Exceptional quotient and transfer of the interval theorem
nodes.statement: Let T be the k-dimensional exceptional subspace, k<n. The quotient map φ_T has triangular minor coordinates and compares H_Q outside T to the quotient height with constant≤(2H_L)^{(8R)ⁿ}. Choose θ_v as the average of the complementary quotient weights and d_{iv}=(n−k)(c_{iv}−θ_v)/n on complementary indices; put Q′=Q^{n/(n−k)}. The quotient is semistable, has at most nRⁿ distinct forms and H_L″≤(2H_L)^{(8R)ⁿ}. For Q>(2H_L)^{200(8R)ⁿ/δ}, H_Q(x)≤Δ^{1/n}Q^{−δ}, x∉T implies H_{Q′}″(φ_Tx)≤(Q′)^{−99δ/(100n)}.
hypotheses: All fields, dimensions, normalizations and strict inequalities are as specified in the statement.
proofSteps: Use the selected restricted minor to eliminate T and bound all quotient coefficients by determinants.
Verify Σθ_v=−w(T)/(n−k)≤0 and normalize the quotient weights; transfer semistability through w(U)−w(T).
Apply the semistable interval result with the reduced dimension and δ′=99δ/(100n). Translate Q′ intervals back to Q and absorb the comparison constants using the stated Q threshold.
acceptance: Check the identity (Q′)^{d_iv}=Q^{c_iv−θ_v} and δ′=99δ/(100n). The quotient dimension is n−k and the conclusion excludes x∈T.

sources.match: The height bound and quotient exponents force a stable low-minimum space above the strict threshold. The relevant mean is over the complement of the selected restriction.

nodes.title: Bounded intervals, systems and final subspace counts
nodes.statement: The parent Parametric Subspace Theorem and its system/interval refinements follow by combining: one exceptional K-subspace; the quotient interval theorem above for x outside it; the elementary short-range gap principle; and the finite system reduction. For each multiplicative interval [Q_h,Q_h^ω), enlarge its endpoints greedily as in EF Lemma 5.2, with the source count and the determinant Δ preserved. The systems statement uses the parent Lemma 5.1 conversion before applying this cover.
hypotheses: All fields, dimensions, normalizations and strict inequalities are as specified in the statement.
proofSteps: Order the interval starts and cover each surviving long interval by short gap ranges. Greedy endpoint extension controls the number without changing the exceptional subspace.
Insert the explicit n,R,δ constants from the parent targets; restriction and quotient losses have already been bounded above.

The classical and p-adic forms, Roth, bounded-degree approximation and Thue–Mahler applications remain parent targets. This node supplies their missing absolute quantitative input rather than redeclaring those targets.
acceptance: Preserve the exceptional subspace, determinant normalization and the parent endpoint conventions while moving between systems, short ranges and long intervals.

sources.match: The local-gap cover and bounded low-height interval are assembled using half-open Q-intervals. These are the interfaces imported by the parent quantitative targets.

nodes.title: Multiprojective degrees and the product criterion
nodes.statement: For an irreducible Z⊂∏P^{n_h} of dimension d, the numbers (Z·L₁^{e₁}⋯L_m^{e_m}) are nonnegative integers for Σe_h=d. For a product Z=∏Z_h only e_h=dim Z_h is nonzero, and that value is∏deg Z_h. Conversely, if Z is not a product, at least two exponent tuples have positive intersection number. For L=Σd_hL_h, (Z·L^d) is the multinomial sum with coefficients d_h^{e_h}.
hypotheses: All fields, dimensions, normalizations and strict inequalities are as specified in the statement.
proofSteps: Iterate the projective-bundle formula to obtain the ambient Chow ring ℤ[L_h]/(L_h^{n_h+1}); apply proper Cartier intersections to effective cycles.

For each projection Z_h=π_hZ choose enough generic hyperplanes to achieve exponent dim Z_h and continue cutting other factors. If Z is not the whole product, Σdim Z_h>dim Z, producing two distinct supported degree tuples.
The geometric argument uses proper projection images and generic hyperplane dimension drops from the lower-tier scheme owner.
acceptance: A product of points has degree 1 and a product of projective spaces has the expected multinomial degree; do not replace multidegree by a single affine polynomial degree.

sources.match: The support and projection-degree inequalities are the geometric input to the product conclusion. General intersection theory remains a requested SF.5 contract.

nodes.title: Weighted jets force local multiplicity
nodes.statement: Work over an algebraically closed characteristic-zero field, with m≥2, positive n_h,d_h, M=Σn_h, σ≥0, 0<ε≤1, and F≠0 multihomogeneous of degrees d_h. Suppose Z is an irreducible component of both index loci Z_σ and Z_(σ+ε), of codimension s≥1. Let π_h project to factors h,…,m, and set δ_h=dim π_h(Z)−dim π_(h+1)(Z), with π_(m+1)(Z) a point. For the localized derivative ideal I defining Z_σ its component multiplicity satisfies m_Z≥(ε/s)^s∏d_h^(n_h−δ_h). If d_h/d_(h+1)≥(mM/ε)^M for all h<m, properly meeting derivative cuts and the multiprojective degree support force Z to be a product.
hypotheses: All fields, dimensions, normalizations and strict inequalities are as specified in the statement.
proofSteps: Localize at Z and use the regular local ring of the smooth multiprojective ambient space in characteristic zero. Ordinary and divided derivatives differ by invertible factorials, so the strict weighted-jet convention gives the same index.
Filter normal variables by the successive projections π_h. Their counts are n_h−δ_h and sum to s. Count monomials in the weighted simplex to get the explicit multiplicity bound.

Use properly meeting derivative cuts with their component lengths and the two positive degree tuples of a nonproduct. The separated d_h make their upper intersection bounds incompatible with the lower multiplicity estimate.
acceptance: Use strict jet vanishing below the index threshold. The component multiplicity bound and the choice of ordinary versus Hasse derivatives must agree in characteristic zero.

sources.locator: Lemma 4, pp. 12–13; Lemma 10 and proof, pp. 23–27
sources.match: The localized index ideal has the stated multiplicity lower bound, with positive block dimensions and degrees. Degree separation then forces the product component.

nodes.title: Fubini–Study Chow height
nodes.statement: For an effective r-cycle Z in Pⁿ over Q̄ with Chow form F_Z, define its normalized Fubini–Study height as the sum over finite places of log coefficient sup norms, plus at infinity the integral of log|F_Z| over r+1 unit spheres with probability measure, plus (r+1)deg(Z)H_n/2, where H_n=Σ_{j=1}^n1/j. Normalize local contributions by [K:ℚ] and archimedean multiplicities. Extend additively to cycles. Multiprojective heights h_L(Z) use the Segre–Veronese metric associated to positive L=O(d₁,…,d_m), with the same point-height normalization. This arithmetic invariant is owned here; generic Chow groups and proper intersections are imported from SF.5.
hypotheses: All fields, dimensions, normalizations and strict inequalities are as specified in the statement.
proofSteps: Construct the incidence Chow form using the generic projective intersection/degree contract requested from SF.5.

Show integrability of log|F_Z| on the spheres and cancellation under rescaling by the product formula. The cited source specifies the height normalization and invokes arithmetic intersection theory; a proof of its analytic/arithmetic Bézout estimates is a recorded gap.
The harmonic term is chosen so a point has log Euclidean projective height. Do not replace this by the logarithm of the coefficient height of the Chow form.
acceptance: Compute [1:1] and P¹ with the sphere-integral harmonic correction. Scalar and finite-extension invariance must hold in this normalization.

sources.match: The sphere-integral cycle-height normalization and product constants are specified here. The full primary proof of the arithmetic intersection input is still the declared gap.

The degree-weighted sum of factor heights must use Fubini–Study point normalization.

nodes.title: Arithmetic cuts and the factor-height estimate
nodes.statement: For the high-index component in the Product Theorem, successive effective Cartier cuts using bounded-height derivatives give the source estimate [k₁:k₀]∏deg Z_h Σ_h d_h h(Z_h)/deg Z_h ≤2(s/ε)^s m^M·M²(Σd_h+log H₂(F)), where M=Σn_h and s=Σcodim Z_h. The geometric degree bound is [k₁:k₀]∏deg Z_h≤(ms/ε)^s. Conjugate components contribute positively; heights are not bounded by degrees alone.
hypotheses: K⊂Q̄ is a number field of coefficients, m≥2, n_h,d_h>0, M=Σn_h, σ≥0 and 0<ε≤1.
F is nonzero of multidegree d; d_h/d_(h+1)≥(mM/ε)^M for h<m.
Z is a common irreducible component of Z_σ and Z_(σ+ε); by the product criterion Z=∏Z_h, with s=Σcodim Z_h≥1 and k₁/k₀ the minimal defining extension.
proofSteps: Construct the truncated effective cycles from successive generic sections, removing components already captured by the index locus.
Bound the height of each derivative by its degree factorial loss and H₂(F); apply arithmetic Bézout in the specified metric, which is the precise recorded source gap.
Sum over the Galois orbit to obtain [k₁:k₀]; keep the factor 1/deg Z_h and the product of all degrees.
acceptance: Keep m^M M², the Galois orbit factor, the product of factor degrees and the division by each factor degree. This node remains conditional on the stated arithmetic Bézout gap.

sources.match: The arithmetic Product Theorem has the same geometric separation hypotheses plus the cycle-height and derivative estimates. Its use remains conditional on the explicitly identified arithmetic Bézout input.

nodes.title: Strict index conclusion at the weak height boundary
nodes.statement: Let m≥2, 0<Θ≤1, F≠0 of binary block degrees d_h>0, and d_h/d_{h+1}≥2m²/Θ. If H₂(x_h)^{d_h}≥(e^{Σd_h}H₂(F))^{(3m²/Θ)^m} for every block, then the index is<mΘ. This is the boundary version used by the parent sharp Roth node: Evertse 1995 states a strict height premise, while the later 1996 lemma uses≥.
hypotheses: All fields, dimensions, normalizations and strict inequalities are as specified in the statement.
proofSteps: Suppose index≥ε=mΘ and put ε′=ε/(m+1). The chain of m+2 index loci gives a repeated irreducible component Z containing the point, of codimension s≥1. Let δ_i be the successive trailing-projection dimension increments.

For the binary factors use the strengthened supported-degree argument of Product Theorem Lemma 11: choose e_i∈{0,1} with positive intersection number, Σe_i=dim Z and η_i=Σ_(j≥i)(δ_j−e_j)≥0. Induct by a generic first-factor cut; on the simultaneous smooth locus the projection dimensions are ranks of coordinate functions, and a cut decreases precisely those ranks spanning the first coordinate. This gives Σ_(i≥2)η_i≥Σdim π_i(Z)−dim Z.

If every individual projection is the whole P¹ then Ση_i≥s. The localized multiplicity bound and the supported-degree intersection bound give 1≤(ms/ε′)^s∏_(i≥2)(d_i/d_(i−1))^η_i≤((m+1)/(2m))^s<1, using s≤m and d_(i−1)/d_i≥2m³/ε. Thus some projection is the point x_h. Its height is bounded above by the mixed cycle height divided by its positive degree.

The coarse arithmetic coefficient is C_s=2m²m![s(m+1)/ε]^s for 1≤s≤m. Since ε≤m, it increases with s. When m=2 its maximum equals 576/ε², so this coarse estimate alone has no slack. Retain the earlier coefficient m²+log 2 from (5.3), since s≤m and log H₂(F)≥0: the sharper maximum is 72(4+log 2)/ε², with ratio (4+log 2)/8<5/8 to (3m³/ε)^m.

For m≥3 the coarse coefficient already suffices: m!≤((m+1)/2)^m gives C_s/(3m³/ε)^m≤2m²((m+1)²/(6m²))^m≤2m²(8/27)^m<1. The last expression is <1 at m=3 and decreases, since its next-term ratio is at most (4/3)²(8/27)<1.

The strict coefficient margin therefore gives a point-height upper bound strictly smaller than the permitted lower bound, even when that lower bound holds with equality. The degree comparison also has explicit strict slack, so no continuity argument at a boundary is required.
acceptance: For m=2 the coarse coefficient ratio is 1; retaining m²+log 2 gives the strict ratio (4+log 2)/8<5/8. The equality boundary remains valid.
The conclusion is strict index<mΘ. No derivative of weight exactly mΘ is required by strict-index vanishing.

sources.match: The sharp Roth inequality follows by the product components and point-height lower bounds, with a strict constant margin.
The weak point-height boundary used by this application is justified by the strict coefficient margin, rather than by a limiting argument at equality.

nodes.title: Rank exactness for the ratio projection
nodes.statement: For Γ⊂(F*)ⁿ of finite rank r and a proper subspace relation involving ℓ≥2 coordinates, let ρ(x)=(x₂/x₁,…,x_ℓ/x₁), Γ₁=im ρ and Γ₂=ker ρ. Then rank Γ₁+rank Γ₂=r, including groups that are not finitely generated. Each nonempty ratio fibre is one coset uΓ₂, with its first ℓ coordinates proportional.
hypotheses: All fields, dimensions, normalizations and strict inequalities are as specified in the statement.
proofSteps: Tensor the exact sequence of abelian groups with ℚ; flatness gives exactness and finite-dimensional rank-nullity gives r=r₁+r₂.
For a fixed ratio choose one representative u and divide every fibre element by u; membership in the kernel is exactly the coordinate-ratio condition.
Do not enumerate a finite generating set for an arbitrary finite-rank group.
acceptance: For the full diagonal subgroup, Γ₁ has rank 0 and Γ₂ has rank r.

nodes.title: Preservation of nondegeneracy after merging a fibre
nodes.statement: Suppose a₁x₁+⋯+a_nx_n=1 is nondegenerate and a minimal homogeneous relation on ℓ coordinates fixes their ratios w_i=x_i/x₁. The merged coefficient b=a₁+Σ_{i=2}^ℓa_iw_i is nonzero; replacing the first ℓ terms by b x₁ gives a nondegenerate equation on n−ℓ+1 coordinates in a coset of Γ₂. The ratio equation on ℓ−1 coordinates is itself nondegenerate after dividing the minimal relation by one term.
hypotheses: All fields, dimensions, normalizations and strict inequalities are as specified in the statement.
proofSteps: A zero b would make an original nonempty subsum vanish. Any vanishing merged subsum expands to an original vanishing subsum.
A minimal relation has no proper zero subsum, so normalizing it gives the required lower-dimensional affine equation. Absorb the chosen fibre representative into its coefficients.
The affine nondegeneracy convention prohibits every nonempty zero subsum, including the full left side; it is not the same as the homogeneous convention.
acceptance: A zero merged coefficient or merged zero subsum expands to an original nonempty zero subsum. The homogeneous minimal relation forbids proper zero subsums.

nodes.title: Unit-equation induction and numerical bounds
nodes.statement: With A(n,r)=exp((6n)^{3n}(r+1)) and B(n,r)=exp((5n)^{3n}(r+1)), the fibre count uses A(ℓ−1,r₁)A(n−ℓ+1,r₂)≤A(n−1,r) for 2≤ℓ≤n and r₁+r₂=r. Covering by B(n,r+1) proper subspaces and selecting at most 2ⁿ minimal zero relations gives 2ⁿA(n−1,r)B(n,r+1)<A(n,r) for n≥2. The coefficient vector may increase the group rank by one; it is not rank-neutral.
hypotheses: All fields, dimensions, normalizations and strict inequalities are as specified in the statement.
proofSteps: Use the rank sum and monotonicity of the explicit exponents to bound the two affine equations in each fibre.
For each proper covering subspace select a support-minimal homogeneous relation, then apply the previous nondegeneracy lemma and induction.
Check the exponential inequality for n=2 directly and use the fast growth of (6n)^{3n} for n>2. The n=1 affine equation has at most one solution.
acceptance: Handle n=1 separately. Check n=2 and rank zero explicitly; multiplying the coefficient vector into the group may add one to the rank.

nodes.title: Cyclic ratio fibres and intersections of progressions
nodes.statement: For φ:ℤ→(F*)^{n−1}, φ(k)=((α₂/α₁)^k,…,(α_n/α₁)^k), every nonempty fibre is a coset of ker φ=dℤ with d≥0. The case d=0 is a singleton, not an empty progression. Finite intersections of such cosets are empty or one coset of the intersection subgroup; for positive moduli the resulting modulus is the lcm. Pullback along a cyclic homomorphism is treated the same way.
hypotheses: All fields, dimensions, normalizations and strict inequalities are as specified in the statement.
proofSteps: Apply subgroup classification in ℤ and coset equality. Use the Chinese-remainder compatibility criterion for nonempty intersections.
Separate zero modulus before taking an lcm; intersecting a singleton with any progression is a singleton or empty.
acceptance: Even integers intersect 3ℤ in 6ℤ.
The fibres of k↦2^k in ℚ* are singletons.
2ℤ and 1+2ℤ have empty intersection.

nodes.title: Simple recurrence zeros from unit fibres
nodes.statement: For a simple recurrence Σ_{i=1}^n a_iα_i^k, α_i distinct nonzero and a_i nonzero, minimal vanishing partitions and the affine unit bound cover the zero set by at most W(n)=exp((6n)^{3n}) arithmetic progressions, including singletons. In the nondegenerate case all progressions are singletons: otherwise restriction to an infinite progression would contradict the Vandermonde determinant for distinct powered roots.
hypotheses: All fields, dimensions, normalizations and strict inequalities are as specified in the statement.
proofSteps: For each support-minimal homogeneous zero relation normalize by one term and apply A(n−1,1). Pull its finite ratio fibres back through the cyclic root-ratio map.
Intersect fibres across the blocks of a vanishing partition; count partitions and use the source numerical inequality giving W(n).
On an infinite progression, powered distinct roots stay distinct under nondegeneracy; evaluating enough consecutive progression points gives an invertible Vandermonde matrix.
acceptance: The sequence 2^k−(−2)^k has the progression 2ℤ of zeros; nondegenerate root ratios instead force every fibre to be a singleton.

nodes.title: Finite-subset reduction to one number field
nodes.statement: For a field K, n≥2 and an integer B≥1, if every finite subset of N⊂Kⁿ lies in at most B proper K-linear subspaces, then N itself has such a cover. Apply this over Q̄ to finite algebraic solution sets with common number fields and constants independent of their degree.
hypotheses: All fields, dimensions, normalizations and strict inequalities are as specified in the statement.
proofSteps: For a finite set M let a(M) be the least sum of dimensions of a B-subspace cover, allowing zero spaces to pad. Every optimal subspace is spanned by points of M, so there are finitely many optimal unordered covers; let b(M) be their positive number.
Choose M₀ maximizing a(M), which is bounded by B(n−1), and then minimizing b(M) among those maxima.

For any finite M⊃M₀, maximality gives a(M)=a(M₀). Every optimal cover of M is an optimal cover of M₀; minimality of b makes the two finite cover sets equal. Apply this to M₀∪{x} for each x∈N; one fixed optimal cover covers all of N.
acceptance: The finite witnesses must span the selected subspaces; a cover depending on the finite subset is sufficient only after proving the extremal-witness argument.

sources.match: The source optimizes the minimum sum of subspace dimensions and then the finite number of optimal covers. This finite-witness argument transfers a uniform cover to arbitrary finite rank.

nodes.title: Symmetric logarithmic seminorm
nodes.statement: For a finite family of real linear forms g_j on ℝʳ, define Ψ(t)=½Σ_j|g_j(t)|. In a finite-rank multiplicative parameterization, g_j are the local coordinate logarithms of chosen independent group elements. The product formula gives Ψ(u)=Σ_i h(α_i(u)) for integer exponent vectors. Ψ is a norm exactly when the common real kernel of the forms is zero.
hypotheses: All fields, dimensions, normalizations and strict inequalities are as specified in the statement.
proofSteps: The triangle inequality and absolute homogeneity follow termwise; zero is equivalent to every summand being zero.
For each multiplicative coordinate, Σ_v log|α_i|_v=0, hence its positive logarithm sum is half its absolute logarithm sum.
acceptance: The empty family gives zero. A family with nonzero common kernel remains only a seminorm, even when no individual form is zero.

sources.match: The symmetric logarithmic function extends from exponent coordinates and satisfies seminorm identities. The packet and suggested file use the same declaration names.

nodes.title: Discreteness forces a genuine real norm
nodes.statement: For multiplicatively independent generators modulo torsion in a fixed number field, the logarithmic seminorm Ψ above has zero real kernel. Fixed-field Northcott and the height-zero torsion criterion first give a positive lower bound on Ψ(u) for nonzero u∈ℤʳ. If the real kernel were nonzero, simultaneous approximation to that kernel direction would produce nonzero integer vectors with Ψ arbitrarily small, a contradiction.

proofSteps: A bounded-height ball in the exponent lattice injects into the fixed-field multiplicative tuple up to the finite torsion kernel.
Use Dirichlet simultaneous approximation on a nonzero real kernel direction and continuity of the finite family of linear forms.
No uniform degree-independent Dobrowolski estimate is used in this step.

nodes.title: Packing cones in the finite-rank logarithmic space
nodes.statement: In a fixed number field let Γ modulo torsion be finitely generated of rank r and let B={u:Ψ(u)≤1}. Fix n≥2 and q=8n. Cover nB by at most (2qn+4)^r=(16n²+4)^r translates ρ+q^−1B, with centers ρ∈(n+1/q)B. For a group point α of h=h(α)>0, its exponent u satisfies Ψ(u)=h_s(α)≤nh, so u/h lies in such a translate and u∈hρ+(h/q)B. Consequently Σ_{v,j}|g_jv(u)−h g_jv(ρ)|≤2h/q. Separate h=0 torsion points; rank zero needs one cone only.
hypotheses: All fields, dimensions, normalizations and strict inequalities are as specified in the statement.
proofSteps: Take a maximal q^−1-separated family in nB. Its disjoint balls of radius 1/(2q) lie in (n+1/(2q))B; the volume ratio bounds its size by (2qn+1)^r, hence by the displayed looser count. Maximality covers nB.
Use h≤h_s≤nh to put u/h in nB. The cone error is Ψ(u−hρ)≤h/q. Because Ψ is half the sum of absolute coordinate logarithms, their summed error is≤2h/q, not h/q.

Torsion is the zero-logarithm case, not a real unit direction. For arbitrary finite-rank groups apply the result to the finitely generated subgroup of each finite subset, then the uniform-cover transfer.
acceptance: Rank zero has one cone; torsion has zero logarithm and does not create a new real direction. Packing uses the norm after its kernel is shown zero.

sources.match: Norm-ball packing covers the logarithmic directions. The radius is reduced by using q=8n to account for the factor two between Ψ and the full absolute logarithmic sum.

nodes.title: Large perturbed unit points have small twisted height
nodes.statement: Let n≥2 and y=αz with α in a fixed cone above, h=h(α)>4n log n, h(z)≤h/(8n), and Σ y_i=1. Set m_jv=g_jv(ρ) for j=1,…,n and m_0v=0. At each place omit a predicted maximizer of m_jv among X₁,…,X_n,ΣX_i, independent of the point within the cone. On the finite logarithmic support S let γ=(Σ_v max_j m_jv)/(n|S|), and give each selected form weight c_jv=m_jv+γ; set other weights zero. Then Σc=0 and Σ|c|≤4n+1. With Q=H(α)^(4n+1), dividing weights by 4n+1 gives twisted height≤Q^−δ for δ=1/(2n(4n+1)); Q>n^(2/δ). Center per place to use the parent EF normalization: the global height is unchanged and Σ_v max_j c′_jv≤1, while the absolute-weight bound need not be preserved by centering. Each cone uses at most 2^(2(2n+9)^2)(8n²+2n)^(n+4) proper subspaces; the complete large-point count multiplies this by (16n²+4)^r.
hypotheses: All fields, dimensions, normalizations and strict inequalities are as specified in the statement.
proofSteps: The cone error gives M=Σ_v max_j m_jv≥1−2/q. Omitting this maximum makes the selected global weight sum −M before adding n|S|γ=M. Every remaining set of n forms is independent.
The selected-weight absolute sum is≤2Σ|m_jv|≤4(n+1/q)≤4n+1. Product-formula weights outside S have zero logarithmic target.
The logarithm of the resulting twisted height is at most h(−1/n+2/(nq)+1/(8n)+2/q)≤−h/(2n), with q=8n. This tracks the factor-two cone error and the perturbation budget.

After weight division Q has the stated exponent; h>4n log n gives its strict large-Q threshold. Subtract the selected mean at each place for EF: these means sum to zero, preserving the global twisted height and controlling the sum of local maxima.
Use the parent quantitative subspace theorem for this fixed form/weight system. Multiply its per-cone count by the corrected cone count; the larger rank factor will be absorbed in the AV final bound.
acceptance: The omitted form depends only on the chosen cone and place. The large-height premise is on α, not y.
For n=2 and q=16 the exponent estimate is −1/4, exactly the required bound. Per-place centering is checked by its sum of maxima, not a claimed unchanged absolute sum.

nodes.title: Toric equation complexity and exceptional locus
nodes.statement: For a proper reduced subvariety V⊂G_mⁿ over Q̄, δ(V) is the least positive degree allowing V to be cut out as a set by polynomials of at most that degree in the fixed projective embedding. δ₀(V) is the analogous incomplete-intersection degree: V is a union of isolated components of such an intersection. V⁰ removes every positive-dimensional torus coset contained in V. For irreducible V, μ_ess(V) is the infimum θ for which the points of height≤θ are Zariski dense. These definitions use h(x)=h(1:x₁:⋯:x_n), not the sum of the scalar heights.
hypotheses: All fields, dimensions, normalizations and strict inequalities are as specified in the statement.
proofSteps: Use the lower-tier variety, isolated-component, degree and stabilizer interfaces requested from SF.5; retain the fixed projective embedding.
Define V⁰ by the union of contained positive-dimensional cosets, rather than deleting every torsion point. The cited proof proves this union is closed via the ensuing descent.
acceptance: The coset x=1 has empty exceptional complement while the hyperplane x+y=1 does not. Heights use the fixed (1:x) embedding.

nodes.title: Hilbert-function lower and fat-point upper bounds
nodes.statement: Let A=K[x₀,…,x_n], with K a field and 0≤r≤min(m,n), and let J be a homogeneous ideal of codimension r containing the intersection of the isolated codimension-r primary components of an ideal generated in degrees d₁≥⋯≥d_m. For ν>Σ_{j≤r}d_j−r, H(A/J;ν)≥deg J·binomial(ν+n−Σ_{j≤r}d_j,n−r). For an irreducible d-dimensional projective V of degree D and positive integral degree ν and fat-point order T≥1, H(V,T;ν)≤binomial(T−1+n−d,n−d)binomial(ν+d,d)D. Use the corrected Chardin–Philippon notion of relative regularity, quantified over all parameter-sequence Koszul complexes; the original reverse implication from the local-cohomology condition to that all-parameter Koszul condition is false.
hypotheses: All fields, dimensions, normalizations and strict inequalities are as specified in the statement.
proofSteps: Import the generic Hilbert polynomial, primary components, Koszul/local-cohomology contracts through explicit lower-tier requests; do not cite higher-tier Heights R09 or Scheme K-theory operations.
Use the corrected relative-regularity lower bound of Chardin–Philippon. Its Corollary 3 remains valid under the published erratum.
For the fat-point upper bound filter by powers of the normal ideal; count monomials in the codimension many normal variables and bound each graded coefficient space by the degree/Hilbert upper bound.
acceptance: Require codim J=r and homogeneous ideals. The binomial lower bound is used only for ν above the stated regularity threshold; the fat-point factor uses codimension, not dimension.

nodes.title: Torsion translation and interpolation determinant
nodes.statement: For irreducible V⊂G_mⁿ and a prime p, compare the monomial evaluation matrix on V with that on ker[p]·V. Its determinant polynomial of degree ν per row has order at least (L−H(V,T;ν))T on the diagonal evaluation locus. The p-adic estimate |1−ζ_p|_p≤p^{−1/(p−1)}, together with the product formula and Hadamard, gives μ_ess(V)≥(1−H(V,T;ν)/H(ker[p]V;ν))T log p/(pν)−n log(ν+1)/(2ν).
hypotheses: The irreducible V is nonempty and ν,T are positive integers. L=H(ker[p]V;ν)>0 is the evaluation-space dimension.
Use the fixed embedding and degree-normalized projective torus height; the determinant bound is allowed to be negative.
proofSteps: Choose monomials forming an evaluation basis on ker[p]V and make the interpolation determinant nonzero by independent evaluations.
At the diagonal, remove at most H(V,T;ν) independent jet rows; the remaining rows each contribute order T.

Translate by p-torsion at a place above p, exploit the local divisibility, and multiply the bounds over every place. Bound archimedean determinant coefficients by Hadamard. This replaces an ineffective gap principle with explicit degree data.
acceptance: The evaluation determinant must be nonzero before taking its height. The ratio H(V,T;ν)/H(ker[p]V;ν) is useful only when strictly below 1.

sources.match: The interpolation matrix has positive degree and dimension parameters. Its determinant height yields the stated multiplicity vanishing bound.

nodes.title: Stabilizers and translation degree control
nodes.statement: For irreducible V and finite H⊂G_mⁿ, deg(HV)=|H/(H∩Stab V)|deg V and δ₀(HV)≤|H/(H∩Stab V)|δ₀(V). For H=ker[p], δ₀(HV)≤pⁿδ₀(V). A prime avoiding the finite component-group index of Stab V gives |H/(H∩Stab V)|≥p^{codim V+1} when V is not a torus coset. Also deg Stab V≤deg V·δ(V)^{dim V}.
hypotheses: Ambient dimension n≥2; the variety is proper and all complexity parameters use the fixed embedding and h(1:x₁:⋯:x_n).
All remaining hypotheses are those in the exact statement.
proofSteps: Distinct irreducible translates are indexed by H/(H∩Stab V), proving the degree formula. For the δ₀ bound start with an intersection X in which V is isolated, and refine it to X′=⋂_(ζ∈H∩Stab V)ζ^−1X. The component V remains isolated, and the stabilizer subgroup preserves X′.

For one representative of each translate class form the product of generic defining equations of its translate of X′. The product degrees are bounded by the number of classes times δ₀(V). Localize around each V-translate; generic choices keep it an isolated component. Merely multiplying unrefined equations would not establish isolation.
For ker[p], the connected stabilizer contributes p^dim Stab V torsion points. If p avoids its finite component-group order and V is not a coset, dim Stab V≤dim V−1, giving the extra p-power.
The stabilizer is cut out by generic translates of the defining equations together with V; the requested generic degree Bézout contract gives deg Stab V≤deg V·δ(V)^dim V.

nodes.title: Explicit small-point cut and relative descent
nodes.statement: For irreducible V of codimension k that is not a torus coset, θ₀=δ₀(V)[27n²log(n²δ₀(V))]^{kn} bounds the degree of a hypersurface containing all its points of height≤θ₀^{−1} without containing V. nodes.title: Coset decomposition with a weighted degree budget
nodes.statement: Let V⊊G_mⁿ be reduced, with components X_k,…,X_n grouped by codimension≥k, and θ=δ(V)[200n⁵log(n²δ(V))]^{(n−k)n(n−1)}. In particular the small points of V⁰ form a finite set of cardinality≤θⁿ.

nodes.title: Small points in a finite-rank thickening
nodes.statement: For Γ of rank r, write Γ_ε={αz:α∈Γ, h(z)≤ε}. For C≥1 and 0≤ε≤(2nθ)^{−1}, #({x∈V⁰∩Γ_ε:h(x)≤C})≤(5nC)^r θ^{n+r}, with θ as above. The estimate is absolute in the degree of the coordinates.

nodes.title: Public conic perturbation cover and the parent ESS budget
nodes.statement: For n≥2 and Γ⊂(Q̄*)ⁿ of finite rank r, all x=αz satisfying Σx_i=1 and h(z)≤(8n)^{−6n³}(1+h(α)) lie in at most (8n)^{6n³(n+r)} proper linear subspaces. nodes.title: Block-constant subalgebra
nodes.statement: For a finite index type I, field F and equivalence relation P on I, B_P is the F-subalgebra of F^I consisting of functions constant on each P-class. It contains the image of the constant scalar functions (isomorphic to F when I is nonempty) and is isomorphic to F^{I/P}. Refining P increases B_P; intersecting such algebras corresponds to the equivalence relation generated by their relations. This light algebra is the stabilizer carrier in the norm-form argument.

A function on I/P pulls back uniquely to a block-constant function; quotient induction gives the algebra equivalence.
Constancy under all relations is constancy under their generated equivalence closure.

nodes.title: Homogeneous unit solutions give finitely many stabilizer cosets
nodes.statement: Let W⊂F^I be a linear subspace and Γ⊂(F*)^I finite rank. Then W∩Γ is contained in finitely many cosets uH_P, where u∈W∩Γ, H_P=Γ∩B_P*, and uB_P⊂W. Finite homogeneous ratios give finitely many normalized patterns, and their common constancy partition is P.

The resulting affine equation is nondegenerate in the ratio-image subgroup, whose rank is finite, so the new refined unit-count theorem gives finitely many coordinate-ratio patterns over F. nodes.title: Galois-stable block algebras descend to subfields
nodes.statement: Embed K into a normal closure F by all ℚ-embeddings, ψ:K→F^I. Let V⊂K be a ℚ-subspace and u=ψ(ξ₀) with ξ₀≠0. Replace P by the equivalence closure of the union of P and all its Galois conjugates so uB_P⊂F⊗V and B_P is Galois-stable under the simultaneous permutation/semilinear action. Its invariants J=B_P^{Gal(F/ℚ)} are a ℚ-subalgebra of K; being a finite-dimensional domain, J is a subfield. One has ξ₀J⊂V, and the coset stabilizer inside O_K* is the unit group of O_J.

nodes.statement: For a finitely generated ℤ-submodule M⊂K and V=ℚM, assume M contains no μO_J with μ∈K* and J⊂K whose ordinary unit group is infinite. nodes.title: Rational polynomial factors in a homogeneous unit relation
nodes.statement: For q≥3 let Γ⊂(Q̄*)^q have finite rank r, z=xy with x∈Γ, y∈(ℚ*)^q and h_proj(y)≤h_proj(x)/(4q²), where h_proj(u)=h(u₁:⋯:u_q) is the degree-normalized homogeneous projective height, and suppose Σz_i=0. nodes.title: Finite obstruction to lowering a progression count
nodes.statement: For Z⊂ℤ a finite union of two-sided arithmetic progressions and singletons, let ν(Z) be its least number of such pieces. There is a finite T⊂ℤ outside Z such that every finite union Z′⊃Z with Z′∩T=∅ satisfies ν(Z′)≥ν(Z). This lower bound, rather than equality for arbitrary supersets, is the contract needed for specialization.
hypotheses: All fields, dimensions, normalizations and strict inequalities are as specified in the statement.
proofSteps: Choose a minimal representation with isolated points Z₁ and periodic part Z₂. For each pair of isolated points, exclude one nonzero-set point on the progression through that pair, so a progression avoiding T contains at most one isolated point.
If Z₂ has period q, put ℓ=qν(Z). In a translated interval of length qℓ disjoint from Z₁, exclude all points outside Z₂. Every progression of modulus≤ℓ avoiding this finite set lies in Z₂.

Suppose Z′ had fewer than ν(Z) pieces. Replace progressions disjoint from Z₂ by their at most one isolated point; enlarge the small-modulus progressions inside Z₂ to moduli dividing q. Their periodic union must fill Z₂: otherwise its density is short by at least 1/q, and the remaining fewer than ν(Z) progressions each have density<1/ℓ.

The periodic pieces therefore need at least ν(Z₂) pieces, and every remaining piece covers at most one isolated point. Their total is at least ν(Z), a contradiction. This proves the stated lower bound.
acceptance: For Z={0} one can take T empty; Z′={0,1} shows why the conclusion is a lower bound rather than equality.
For Z=2ℤ∪3ℤ, the obstruction protects a least cover by two independent moduli; it does not prescribe one common modulus.

nodes.title: Refined counts for multiple-root recurrences
nodes.statement: Let a nonzero recurrence over an algebraically closed characteristic-zero field have minimal order t≥1, k distinct nonzero roots and maximum root multiplicity a. Its integer zero set is a union of at most exp(exp(70t)) arithmetic progressions, including singletons. If no quotient of distinct roots is a root of unity, it has at most (8k^a)^{8k^{6a}} zeros, also≤exp(32a k^{6a}log k) for k≥2. For k=1 there are at most a−1 zeros. No common progression modulus is required.
hypotheses: All fields, dimensions, normalizations and strict inequalities are as specified in the statement.
proofSteps: Expand the coefficient polynomials in a Q-basis to get independent forms; fewer than a exceptional indices make all coefficient polynomials vanish.
On a class x=x₀+my, replace roots by α_i^m. In the torsion case split into at most ℏ^{−1} residue classes and merge equal powered roots, decreasing t.

In the non-torsion case use degree lowering. An infinite progression from a lower-degree auxiliary equation need not be wholly inside the original zero set: restrict the original equation to it and merge equal powered roots before the second induction. This explains the square in Z(t,T).
The general induction uses Z(t,T)=(8T)^{(2^t−1)8T⁵}; the nondegenerate induction uses (8T)^{8T⁵t} without the square. Substitute T≤e^{12t} or T≤k^a respectively.

First transfer the nondegenerate bound to arbitrary characteristic-zero coefficients using Schmidt1999 §2, Lemma 1, pp.246–247. The rank-deficiency equations for a nonzero polynomial vector vanishing on its whole zero set define a variety over ℚ, even for an infinite zero set, by Noetherianity. On a ℚ-irreducible component of degree A, generic rational linear sections give an algebraic point of degree≤A outside any finite union of proper closed subsets.

The root-ratio hypersurface for exact torsion order m forces point degree≥φ(m). Since φ(m)→∞, only finitely many such hypersurfaces can contain a point of degree≤A. Exclude these finitely many and the zero-root locus before taking the section. Solve the remaining nonzero coefficient kernel over its number field. This preserves all original zeros and nondegeneracy, without claiming to preserve every nonzero value.

For general roots, let q be the lcm of the orders of torsion root ratios. On each residue modulo q merge equal powered roots. Either the merged coefficient polynomials all vanish identically, yielding a whole progression, or their non-torsion ratios and the just-transferred nondegenerate theorem give finitely many zeros. This establishes qualitative SML within this proof, before using it in specialization.

Apply the finite-progression-obstruction node to that zero set. The parent specialization lemma, with inverses of the roots, leading coefficients and finitely many values indexed by T adjoined, preserves the order and those nonzero values; every original zero is preserved by the ring homomorphism. The specialized zero set contains the original and avoids T, so its least progression count is at least the original count. Apply the algebraic general bound. The finitely generated coefficient field embeds in ℂ, extending the argument to any characteristic-zero field.
acceptance: For (1−ζ_r^x)(1−ζ_s^x), gcd(r,s)=1, the zero set is rℤ∪sℤ and need not admit a small equal-modulus representation.
For (x−3)2^x, k=1,a=2 and the zero set is the singleton {3}.

nodes.title: Height zero in a number field is torsion
nodes.statement: For x∈K* in a number field, absolute logarithmic height h(x)=0 if and only if x has finite multiplicative order. Only the fixed-field assertion is needed to prove the real logarithmic norm has zero kernel.
hypotheses: All fields, dimensions, normalizations and strict inequalities are as specified in the statement.
proofSteps: If h(x)=0, all positive powers have height zero by the native power identity; fixed-field Northcott makes them a finite set. Two powers coincide, so x has finite order.
Conversely a nonzero power equal to 1 and the power identity imply h(x)=0.

nodes.title: Polynomial-geometric basis from finite differences
nodes.statement: For distinct nonzero α_i and multiplicities t_i>0 over a characteristic-zero field, the sequences k↦k^jα_i^k, 0≤j<t_i, are linearly independent and annihilated by ∏_i(shift−α_i)^{t_i}. They form a basis of the native solution space for that companion polynomial, of dimension Σt_i.
hypotheses: All fields, dimensions, normalizations and strict inequalities are as specified in the statement.
proofSteps: The operator shift−α lowers the degree of P(k)α^k by one when its root matches; for a different root it preserves the leading degree with nonzero leading scalar.
To isolate one root group apply the annihilators of all other groups. A nonzero polynomial over a characteristic-zero field cannot vanish at all natural integers, proving independence.
The native solution-space rank then gives spanning. Invertible constant coefficient allows extension backwards without a generic Jordan-form dependency.
acceptance: For (X−2)² the basis is 2^k and k2^k. Distinct-root annihilators preserve the other polynomial leading degree; the dimension is the sum of multiplicities.

nodes.title: Explicit non-torsion height and conjugacy-class refinement
nodes.statement: For a nonzero algebraic number β that is not a root of unity, of degree d≥2, d h(β)>(1/4)(log log d/log d)³. The weaker bound h(β)≥1/(4d(log⁺d)³), with log⁺x=max(1,log x), also includes d=1 by h(β)≥log 2. If its d conjugates form m equal-size classes modulo roots of unity, then h(β)≥1/(4d(log⁺m)³): the product of one class has degree≤m, is not torsion and has height≤(d/m)h(β). This is the quantitative height input for Schmidt’s conjugate selection.
hypotheses: All fields, dimensions, normalizations and strict inequalities are as specified in the statement.
proofSteps: For Voutier’s bound, first reduce nonintegral numbers using their leading coefficient and reduce degree when powering causes conjugate collisions. For the remaining integral case form the confluent Vandermonde matrix at conjugates and their first-prime powers, with multiplicities k and 1.

Its square is a nonzero rational integer. The determinant product formula and Fermat congruences give divisibility by (p₁⋯p_s)^{2dk}; discriminant factors supply the second lower bound. Hadamard and the factorial product give the upper bound in terms of the Mahler measure.

Compare the two bounds with (k,s)=(7,11),(8,14),(7,17) in the finite degree ranges, and k≈k₁ log d/log log d, s≈s₁(log d/log log d)² for d>10000. The primary proof was read; its external prime estimates, Odlyzko bound, degree-reduction lemma and low-degree computations remain the explicit gap, rather than pretending they follow from Northcott.

For the weaker degree estimate, Voutier gives the implication directly when d≥16 since log log d≥1. For 2≤d≤15 separately use the stated low-degree Mahler-measure input and certify its comparisons to 1/(4(log⁺d)³); d=1 uses log 2. These low-degree verifications are included in the declared external-input gap.

For the class refinement use Galois transitivity to prove equal class sizes. The class product has at most m conjugates; if it were torsion, β^{d/m} would be torsion. Apply the weaker degree bound to this product and divide its upper height estimate by d/m.

The class-product degree can be 1: include the rational lower bound log 2.
